 EPFO Cannot Recover Dues From Personal Guarantor's Exhausted Estate: NCLT Hyderabad
 Mohd.Rehan Ali 
 18 Nov 2026 7:12 PM IST
 Share this 
 The National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT), Hyderabad, has held that a statutory claim, however high its priority under law, cannot be recovered from a bankruptcy estate that has already been exhausted and distributed among creditors.
 The Bench of Judicial Member Rajeev Bhardwaj and Technical Member Sanjay Puri observed, "In the absence of any surviving assets or funds in the Bankruptcy Trust account of the Personal Guarantor, this Tribunal cannot issue a mechanical direction to Respondent No. 1 for payment or satisfaction of any dues. A statutory claim, however high its priority in law, cannot be satisfied out of an estate that holds no realisable value" 
 The tribunal made the observation while dismissing an application filed by the Employees' Provident Fund Organisation (EPFO), which sought consideration and admission of its ₹1.12 crore provident fund claim against GKC Projects Limited.
 The claim comprised ₹90.51 lakh in damages under Section 14B and interest under Section 7Q of the Employees' Provident Funds and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952, for December 2008 to November 2018. It also involved another ₹1.48 lakh in damages and ₹1.50 lakh in interest for March 2019 to December 2023. This was all along with ₹18.79 lakh in provident fund contributions up to February 2023.
 EPFO argued that provident fund dues enjoy statutory priority under Sections 8B to 8G and 11 of the EPF Act. It also relied on Sections 36(4)(a)(iii) and 155(2) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC), which exclude provident fund, pension fund, and gratuity fund dues from the liquidation and bankruptcy estates, respectively.
 The Bankruptcy Trustee submitted that the personal guarantor's properties in Ameerpet and Guttala Begumpet had been auctioned for ₹5.72 crore and ₹2.05 crore, respectively. The sale proceeds had been distributed among creditors, leaving no funds in the Bankruptcy Trust account.
 The tribunal noted that EPFO's dues had been assessed against GKC Projects, whose resolution plan, submitted by SMC Infrastructures Private Limited, was approved on March 30, 2021. EPFO had received an allocation of 1% towards its claim under the resolution plan.
 If aggrieved by this allocation, EPFO's appropriate remedy was to file a timely statutory appeal against the approval of the resolution plan, the tribunal observed.
 It further noted that the corporate debtor and its personal guarantor are distinct legal entities. While a guarantor's liability is co-extensive with that of the principal debtor, recovery in personal bankruptcy proceedings under Part III of the IBC is confined to the individual estate of the bankrupt.
 The tribunal also took note of the Bankruptcy Trustee's application seeking the personal guarantor's discharge under Section 138(1)(a) of the IBC. The application was supported by institutional financial creditors holding 72% of the voting share.
 Holding that the estate had been completely exhausted and the sale proceeds distributed, the tribunal said the relief sought against the Bankruptcy Trustee could not be given effect. It accordingly dismissed EPFO's application as infructuous.
 For Applicant: Advocate Vinod Pasala and V. Venu Madhava Swamy
 For Respondents: Advocate M. Maharshi Viswaraj; Bankruptcy Trustee DSRK Sai Baba
